newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right sits out by-election run-off.
newsitem.headline: French right sits out by-election run-off.

text.p: France's ruling centre-right chose on Monday to endorse neither candidate in a southern parliamentary by-election run-off between a Communist and a candidate from the extreme-right National Front.
"How can you choose between the plague and cholera?" asked Pierre-Andre Wiltzer, spokesman for the centrist Union for French Democracy, junior partner in the ruling coalition.
In two local by-election run-offs last month, centre-right candidates edged out the National Front with leftwing support after the left failed to make it past the first round of voting.
Monday's announcement signalled that the centre-right would not return the favour when it was the rightist who suffered a first-round defeat.

Former Prime Minister Edouard Balladur, of the Gaullist Rally For the Republic, senior coalition partner, said the vote highlighted a deep moral crisis in the country. "The (ruling coalition) must recover...This vote is in a way an appeal" to ruling parties, he told France-3 television.
He said he supported the decision to endorse neither candidate in the second round.

In Sunday's contest to succeed disgraced former businessman and soccer boss Bernard Tapie in parliament, voters will choose between Gardanne's Communist mayor Roger Mei and Damien Barriler of Jean-Marie Le Pen's anti-immigrant National Front party.

The by-election in the depressed working-class town of Gardanne near Marseille in southern France is widely seen as illustrating the weakness of the mainstream left and right parties 18 months before the 1998 general election.
The Communist-National Front run-off is a major embarrassment for France's mainstream politicians, suggesting that they have no answer to voters' main concerns.
The candidates of the mainstream right and left finished third and fourth in Sunday's first-round ballot, both failing to qualify for the run-off.
In contrast to the centre-right, the opposition Socialists and the Greens party have urged their voters to support the Communist candidate to prevent a National Front victory.

Both Communists and extreme rightists feed on fears of unemployment -- the coal mine that is Gardanne's biggest employer with 4,000 jobs is due to close in 2005 -- and immigration, especially after recent incidents of racial violence in neighbouring Marseille.
Tapie won the seat in 1993 for the small left-wing Radical movement with Socialist backing with 25 percent of the vote.
The fast-talking entrepreneur hardly ever returned to his constituency and was stripped of his seat after being ruled bankrupt and convicted of fraud, tax evasion and bribery.
